paper.title: The role of task breadth and cognitive flexibility in generative AI-supported creative idea generation
paper.pdf_filename: Sorin et al (2026) - The role of task breadth and cognitive flexibility in generative AI-supported cr.pdf
paper.version_read: Published journal version: Technovation 153 (2026) 103540; received 11 November 2025, revised 3 March 2026, accepted 16 March 2026, available online 19 March 2026 (PDF p. 1).
paper.one_line_finding: Seeing GPT-3-generated startup ideas raised breadth of exploration in the broad Study 1 task (2.32 vs 1.60 categories, d = 0.67, Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.01; p. 8, Section 4.6.1; Table 4, p. 9) and lowered similarity among participants' first ideas (0.74 vs 0.81, permutation p = 0.00; Table 7, p. 11), but showed no statistically significant difference in either in the narrow Study 2 EdTech task (breadth 1.39 vs 1.38, p = 1.00, p. 10, Section 5.5.1; Table 6; similarity 0.87 vs 0.87, p = 0.09, Table 7; p. 11); untested expert creativity means were 4.23 vs 4.35 in Study 1 and 4.86 vs 4.52 in Study 2 (Appendix D, p. 18).

studies.label: Study 1 (broad startup idea task, master's students)

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 6, Section 4.1 (randomized); PDF p. 8, Section 4.6 (analyzed)
counts_source.quote:
Ninety-three participants were randomly assigned to one of two groups: exposed to ideas generated by a fine-tuned LLM (n = 46) or no exposure to LLM-generated ideas (n = 47).
In total, 90 participants (45 per group) generated 208 ideas.

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Ten ideas randomly drawn from the GPT-3 startup-idea database were displayed during ideation as optional inspiration; copying an identical idea was prohibited. Internet research was permitted in both arms (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3; PDF p. 14, Appendix B).

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same broad startup scenario and Qualtrics interface, without AI-generated ideas; internet research was permitted (PDF p. 7, Section 4.2; PDF p. 14, Appendix B).

studies.task: International management master's students with prior entrepreneurship coursework proposed startup ideas in any domain for an incubator, describing the business need, product or service, revenue source and target customer (PDF pp. 6-8, Sections 4.1-4.5).

ai_tool.name: GPT-3, used through Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI; described as a fine-tuned startup-idea generator
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 6, Section 4.2: GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020); Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI (2022). Year records the underlying GPT-3 model citation; the product is cited separately as 2022.

preregistration.where: No preregistration reported in the article or appendices; an a priori power analysis is reported in Section 4.1 (PDF p. 6).

studies.label: Study 2 (narrow EdTech startup idea task, Prolific UK entrepreneurs)

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 9, Section 5.1 (randomized arm counts); Section 5.5 (analyzed counts)
counts_source.quote:
use of LLM-generated ideas (n = 60) versus no use (n = 60).

arms.name: LLM-assisted human
arms.description: Four randomly selected education-related ideas from the same GPT-3 generator were displayed during ideation, labeled as AI suggestions that participants could ignore (PDF p. 9, Sections 5.2-5.3; PDF p. 14, Appendix B).

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Same technology-in-education startup task without AI-generated suggestions (PDF p. 14, Appendix B).

studies.task: Prolific UK panel members who self-declared entrepreneurship or business ownership proposed technology-in-education startup ideas specifying the need, customer, technological solution and revenue source (PDF p. 9, Sections 5.1-5.4; PDF p. 14, Appendix B).

ai_tool.name: GPT-3, used through Startup Ideas powered by OpenAI; the same startup-idea generator as Study 1, with education-related stimuli
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 6, Section 4.2: GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), product cited as 2022; PDF p. 9, Section 5.2, selection of education-related ideas from the fine-tuned LLM.

preregistration.where: No preregistration reported in the article or appendices; Section 5.1 (PDF p. 9) invokes the power considerations of Study 1.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of distinct semantic categories spanned by each participant's ideas; an author and an independent researcher coded the outputs and breadth scores were averaged across raters (PDF p. 7, Section 4.4.1; Appendix C).

sources.locator: PDF p. 9, Table 4, Breadth of Exploration (columns M, SD, N, d)
sources.quote: Breadth of Exploration LLM-assisted human 2.32 1.32 45 0.67 Human-only 1.60 0.74 45
experimental condition on breadth of exploration (χ2(1) = 6.43, p = 0.01)
In total, 90 participants (45 per group) generated 208 ideas.

estimates.notes: Kruskal-Wallis statistic is printed as chi-squared. Cohen's d is transcribed without changing its sign; its standardizer is not specified. The paper says parametric tests give the same conclusion but supplies no additional statistics. This is the paper's hypothesized primary outcome; breadth measures within-person category exploration and is coded flexibility, not across-person diversity. Dropping participants who failed the manipulation check reportedly leaves the finding unchanged; no numbers are printed for that restricted analysis. The significance is said to survive a Holm–Bonferroni correction, but no adjusted p-value is printed (PDF p. 8, Section 4.6.1).

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of ideas generated divided by the participant's breadth of exploration: ideas per explored semantic category, interpreted as depth or persistence (PDF p. 8, Section 4.4.2; for Study 2, PDF p. 9, Section 5.4).

sources.quote: Depth of Exploration LLM-assisted human 1.13 0.26 45 0.07 Human-only 1.15 0.33 45
LLM assistance did not significantly affect depth of exploration (χ2(1) = 0.45, p = 0.50)

estimates.notes: Kruskal-Wallis statistic is printed as chi-squared. Cohen's d is transcribed without changing its sign; its standardizer is not specified. The paper says parametric tests give the same conclusion but supplies no additional statistics. Higher values mean more ideas per explored category (greater depth/persistence), not necessarily greater creative quality. The paper includes depth in its primary checks but states no hypothesis for it; construct other keeps it outside pooled creativity estimates. The printed d is positive although the displayed LLM-assisted mean is lower than the Human-only mean; no correction has been made.

estimates.outcome: Within-condition semantic similarity among participants' ideas
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Average pairwise cosine similarity between sentence embeddings of ideas within each condition, using SpaCy (embedding model not named). Preprocessing includes tokenization, stop-word and generic-word removal, lemmatization and punctuation removal (PDF p. 8, Section 4.6.2). Only each participant's first idea was retained.

stats.difference_is: Human-only minus LLM-assisted human (control minus treatment), as indicated by the ordering and printed means; retained as printed.

sources.locator: PDF p. 11, Table 7, Study 1 rows (columns M and SD; N is labeled ideas)
sources.quote: Study 1 LLM-assisted human 0.74 0.13 45 0.00 Study 1 Human-only 0.81 0.08 45
(M difference = 0.07, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.04, 0.10], p = 0.00, Cohen's d = 0.91).
In total, 90 participants (45 per group) generated 208 ideas.
Based on permutation tests with 10,000 iterations

estimates.notes: Exploratory group-level analysis. The test is a permutation test; no separate test statistic or SE is printed. The reported SDs are retained with sd_level null because the paper does not say whether they describe pairs or idea-level summaries. The analysis averages all within-condition pairs; the number of pairs is not printed, so n_units is null. The permutation resampling unit and handling of pairs sharing people are unspecified, so se_basis is unclear under extraction-spec.md, Field notes, and creativity-codebook.md, Section 10; this record is not pooled. The pairwise outcome unit does not establish that pairs were treated as independent observations. The reported confidence interval and p-value are retained; not_reported would be inaccurate because contrast uncertainty is printed. Cohen's d standardizer is not stated. No direction or uncertainty was recomputed. The printed positive difference and d correspond to greater similarity in Human-only, whereas lower similarity in the assisted arm indicates greater diversity. The p-value is retained as printed (0.00), without inferring an exact probability or bound.

not_extracted.what: S1-O8: semantic similarity of the LLM-generated stimulus pool versus Human-only outputs; related model-pool preprocessing comparison
not_extracted.reason: The stimulus pool contains model-only outputs, with no person working in that arm. It is not an eligible randomized human-assistance contrast (PDF p. 7, Section 4.2; PDF p. 8, Section 4.6.2).

not_extracted.what: S2-O8: semantic similarity of the LLM-generated education stimulus pool versus Human-only outputs; descriptive comparisons with participant outputs
not_extracted.reason: The stimulus pool contains model-only outputs rather than human task responses; the paper also distinguishes the pool's broader education topic from the EdTech task. No eligible human-assistance contrast is supplied by the pool comparisons (PDF p. 10, Section 5.5.2).

not_extracted.what: Idea length/elaboration: statement that AI-exposed participants produced shorter ideas
not_extracted.reason: Appendix D presents this as a plausible explanation but gives no study attribution, measurement procedure, analysis unit, sample or numerical contrast. It cannot be assigned to a study without inventing provenance (PDF p. 19, Appendix D, Interpretation).

not_extracted.what: S1: manipulation-check understanding that supplied ideas came from AI
not_extracted.reason: Participant self-report about recognizing the manipulation, not a measure scored on creative output (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3).

not_extracted.what: S2: manipulation-check understanding that supplied ideas came from AI
not_extracted.reason: Participant self-report about recognizing the manipulation, not a measure scored on creative output (PDF p. 9, Section 5.3).

not_extracted.what: S1: breadth by manipulation-check response and sensitivity analysis excluding participants who failed that check
not_extracted.reason: Subgroup comparison and restricted-sample analysis rather than a full-sample randomized-arm contrast; only qualitative conclusions are printed (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3).

not_extracted.what: S2: breadth by manipulation-check response and sensitivity analysis excluding participants who failed that check
not_extracted.reason: Subgroup comparison and restricted-sample analysis rather than a full-sample randomized-arm contrast; only qualitative conclusions are printed (PDF p. 9, Section 5.3).
Scenario-development samples provided open-ended feedback; no randomized generative-AI assistance contrast or eligible scored outcome is reported (PDF p. 7, Section 4.3).

not_extracted.what: S1/S2 breadth and depth: alternative parametric tests; S2 analysis reincluding excluded observations
not_extracted.reason: These are alternative analyses of the same arm-outcome comparisons already extracted. The paper reports only unchanged qualitative conclusions, without separate numerical contrasts or analysis counts; they are documented in the existing estimate notes rather than duplicated as additional estimates (PDF p. 8, Section 4.6.1; PDF p. 9, Section 5.1; PDF p. 10, Section 5.5.1).

Task breadth was varied across separate samples, not randomized between people within one experiment; differences across the two studies do not supply an eligible causal contrast. Both within-study AI-assistance contrasts are retained (PDF p. 6, Section 3.3; PDF pp. 10-11, Section 5.5.3; PDF p. 13, Section 7).

not_extracted.what: Appendix E Shapiro-Wilk tests and kernel density plots
not_extracted.reason: Distributional diagnostics, not AI-arm contrasts on creative output. No graph values are digitized (PDF p. 19, Appendix E).

These tables document the coding taxonomy across the idea pools and do not report arm-specific category-frequency contrasts. The participant-level breadth and depth outcomes using the taxonomy are extracted (PDF pp. 15-18, Appendix C).

open_items: Study 2 prints randomized arm counts but no combined randomized total. n_randomized is null at study level to avoid deriving a count; both arm counts are retained (PDF p. 9, Section 5.1).

For both similarity outcomes, the SD unit, permutation resampling unit, handling of pairs sharing participants and Cohen's d standardizer are unspecified. Participant-level uncertainty cannot be confirmed from the printed report (PDF pp. 8, 10-11).
Study 2 similarity: confirm the subtraction order and unrounded means behind the positive reported difference when both displayed arm means are equal (PDF p. 10, Section 5.5.2; PDF p. 11, Table 7).
Study 2 similarity: confirm that the first-idea rule was used; the paper says the analyses were parallel to Study 1 without restating selection (PDF p. 10, Section 5.5.2).
Study 1 usefulness and creativity: clarify whether the usefulness item described as dropped after Study 1 is included in the reported averages (PDF p. 18, Appendix D).
Study 2 breadth/depth: clarify how the out-of-instruction-scope category is treated in the main analysis despite the stated exclusions (PDF p. 9, Sections 5.1 and 5.4; PDF p. 16, Appendix C).
Per-arm exclusion reasons are not separately printed. The randomized and analyzed arm counts are retained without calculating exclusion counts (PDF pp. 6, 8-9).
Study 1 recruitment country is not reported; international-student status and language choices do not establish country (PDF p. 6, Section 4.1).

Possible sample overlap with c917 and the cited Sorin and Pagani chapter remains unconfirmed. The reconciled form identifies these leads, but this PDF identifies no shared participants; shared_sample remains null (PDF p. 13, Acknowledgements; PDF p. 20, References).

The qualitative shorter-ideas statement needs study attribution, a length definition, aggregation unit, analyzed sample and numerical results before it can become an elaboration estimate (PDF p. 19, Appendix D).
The denominator used for each printed Cohen's d is not defined (PDF p. 9, Table 4; PDF p. 11, Table 6; PDF pp. 8 and 10, similarity results).
